title: The cobra's shade
hookLine: tradition says that as he slept in the fields a cobra spread its hood to shade his face
last: THE BOY AND THE TEACHER — ASK WHAT IT MEANS.

lines: A HOT AFTERNOON IN THE PASTURES.
cards: A hot afternoon in Punjab, the kind of heat that flattens everything; even the birds go quiet. In the pastures beyond Talwandi, a teenage boy has been sent to watch the family's buffaloes.
His father hopes the job will teach him some responsibility. But the boy has found a tree, lain down beneath it, and fallen asleep in the heat. The sun moves.
The shade slides off his face. And then, the story says, something comes out of the grass.

teach.b: Here's the story the janamsakhis tell. A cobra slides up beside the sleeping boy, raises itself, and spreads its hood wide over his face like a small umbrella, keeping him in shade.
Just then Rai Bular, the Muslim landlord of Talwandi, comes riding past. He sees the boy, the snake, the hood. He doesn't reach for a stick.
He understands, the story says, that he's looking at someone the world itself is protecting.

From that day Rai Bular is remembered as one of the first to honor Nanak, and he defended the boy to his worried father more than once. A gurdwara in Nankana Sahib marks the place tradition connects with the story.

teach.h: HISTORY OR SAKHI? SOURCES CAN'T SAY.
teach.b: The sources can't say, and it's honest to admit that. Many Sikhs treasure it as a true event. Many others, and many historians, hear it as a sakhi: a story told to show something true.
And what it shows is lovely.
A cobra is the most dangerous creature in the field, and here the dangerous thing becomes the shelter.
Something out there, even something fierce, is looking after the boy.
Sikhs speak of God as the protector who keeps the ones who remember, and the story puts that in a single picture: a hood spread wide over a sleeping face.
Plenty of people have known something like it: a thing that could have gone wrong and didn't, a shelter they didn't arrange.

how: Sikhs tell the story of the cobra's shade as a sakhi of Guru Nanak's youth, and pilgrims to Nankana Sahib visit the gurdwara that tradition connects with it.

o: a snake, like the cobra that shaded Nanak
a herd of buffaloes out at pasture
the shade of a tree in the midday heat

p: spread its hood over his face

he stopped, and understood the boy was being protected.
Rai Bular went on to defend Nanak to his father

games.q: you're Rai Bular, riding past. a cobra has its hood spread over a sleeping boy's face. what do you do?
o: grab a stick and drive the snake off.
stop, and see that the boy is being protected.
ride on. it's none of your business.
games.why: the story says he stopped and understood, and from then on he honored the boy.

practice: If you can, move into some shade: a tree, a porch, the cool side of a room, or close your eyes and picture that tree in Punjab. Let your body rest completely.
Bring to mind one time you were protected without arranging it, a near miss or a stranger's help, and let yourself feel sheltered.

wordCard.voice: Sapp. The cobra that spread its hood over the sleeping Nanak to shade him, and the landlord, Rai Bular, who saw it and understood.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: sapp, a snake.

carryVoice: Your line: something shelters you. Even when you didn't arrange it, and didn't see it coming. That's day twenty-five.
